summary: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].
title: KlaskTron: An Open-Source Platform for Physical Adversarial Multi-Agent RL

summary: Bridges are critical transportation infrastructure, and reliable operation and maintenance (O&M) is essential for traffic safety and long-term structural performance. However, bridge O&M faces key bottlenecks: no unified architecture coordinates heterogeneous resources; model inferences lack clear links to physical-mechanical laws; and experts' tacit knowledge remains difficult to formalize. This study proposes a knowledge-enhanced autonomy formalization methodology and apply it to construct the Bridge O&M Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System (BOMMA), which integrates heterogeneous diagnostic actions, physics-mechanics-informed representations, long-term memory, and structured experiential knowledge within a coordinated multi-agent workflow, enabling interpretable and traceable scheduling, analysis, and decision-making. On 3,492 multi-source instructions, the proposed method achieves scheduling recalls of 85.37% for simple and 99.40% for composite tasks, with 95.35% BERT F1-score for O&M action reasoning. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of the components in the autonomy. This study bridges general LLM reasoning and specialized bridge O&M requirements.
title: Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System for Bridge Operation and Maintenance based on Large Language Model

summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), and they introduce the risk of coordination among agents that might escape human oversight. The J-space has been used to uncover deception in single LLMs, but its use for uncovering and steering collusion between agents remains unexplored. We show, with interpretability experiments on DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) on the NARCBench collusion benchmark, that colluding agents' J-space holds the collusion itself: before replying, 86% of colluders represent misrepresentation, concealment or remorse. In a steganographic card-counting task, the receiver's J-space holds a hidden count, and causal interventions alter its count. We also introduce the Jacobian Pair Contrast (J-PACT), an unsupervised method for detecting collusion between agents. We evaluate J-PACT on four open-weight models: GPT-OSS-20B, Llama-3.3-70B-IT, Qwen3-32B, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B). J-PACT retains 85% of the above-chance AUROC of supervised NARCBench probes, matches them on steganographic scenarios, and names the colluding pair up to its complement in 99% of detected runs.
title: Multi-Agent Collusion and the J-Space

summary: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. summary: Wave energy converters (WECs) are typically designed to operate near resonance to maximize energy capture. While this enhances power absorption, it also amplifies structural loads and accelerates fatigue damage. As a result, fatigue becomes a critical design driver even when stress remains below material yield limits. Fatigue in offshore systems has been widely studied, particularly under variable-amplitude loading induced by waves, wind, and currents. These effects are commonly evaluated using the Palmgren–Miner damage accumulation rule, where failure is predicted once cumulative damage reaches unity. However, fatigue assessment for WECs remains less developed, especially in terms of linking environmental conditions to structural degradation and operational stress limits. The objective of this work is to evaluate, predict and improve confidence in the structural response and fatigue life of a WEC under representative operating conditions and to identify critical components and failure modes before deployment in March 2026 accounting for not only load and geometric factors, but also environmental conditions such as temperature.
title: Worst-Case Fatigue Life of an OSWEC Under Sustained Sea States

summary: This repository presents an evidence-anchored, discipline-sensitive multicriteria assessment framework designed to support transparent, accountable, and reproducible evaluations of academic distinction and research integrity. The framework comprises a Microsoft Excel workbook organized into seven disciplinary classes corresponding to those of the European Academy of Sciences and Arts (EASA): 1. Humanities 2. Medicine 3. Arts 4. Natural Sciences 5. Social Sciences 6. Environmental and Technical Sciences 7. World Religions Each disciplinary class includes ten weighted assessment criteria evaluated on a five-level ordinal scale (0–4). Weighted scores are aggregated and normalized against the maximum attainable score for each class, generating percentage-based results and illustrative classification guidance. The workbook contains 15 worksheets, including discipline-specific evaluation forms, a scoring protocol, research integrity resources, an integrity register, a reusable audit template, and guidance for nominators. A central feature of the framework is the separation of academic merit assessment from research integrity verification. The integrity workflow supports the documentation and contextual examination of retractions, expressions of concern, citation irregularities, potential publication anomalies, and editorial or peer-review conflicts of interest. The framework distinguishes between unverified allegations, documented concerns, and substantiated findings. Bibliometric anomalies, retractions, or incomplete verification procedures must not automatically be interpreted as proof of individual research misconduct. The workbook also incorporates guidance for nominators regarding documentary evidence and the distinction between achievements that are not documented, criteria that have not yet been assessed, and verified absence of specific achievements. The assessment framework is intended to facilitate structured scholarly judgment rather than replace it. Its numerical weights and classification thresholds are illustrative methodological parameters and have not undergone independent empirical validation. Scope and limitations The instrument is proposed for academic discussion, methodological evaluation, pilot testing, and potential institutional adaptation. It is not an autonomous research misconduct detection system or a validated psychometric instrument. The workbook does not independently retrieve or verify bibliometric information. External sources require manual verification or separately implemented data-population procedures. The framework was independently developed with reference to the seven disciplinary classes of EASA. It does not constitute an officially adopted assessment policy of the European Academy of Sciences and Arts (EASA) or the World Academy of Art and Science (WAAS). Reproducibility and responsible use The accompanying README provides methodological information, scoring instructions, evidence requirements, research integrity safeguards, and limitations. Users are encouraged to document the evidence supporting individual scores, distinguish missing information from verified negative findings, and ensure independent review and appropriate procedural fairness before making consequential decisions. This Version 1.0 is provided as a transparent and reusable methodological resource for further examination, testing, and refinement. Contents: the revised manuscript (PDF) and the CSV files of every plotted series and table, in the format of the author's dark matter flow datasets. Pair statistics from the Virgo SCDM N-body simulation at redshifts z = 10 to 0. Companion datasets: Part I (halo-based) doi:10.5281/zenodo.6541231 , Part II (correlation-based) doi:10.5281/zenodo.6757654 . Major findings (Virgo SCDM N-body simulation, redshifts z = 10 to 0): Kinematic relations of any order are derived for incompressible, constant-divergence and irrotational flow, and validated by the simulation. On large scales, third-order velocity correlations can be related to the density correlation or the pairwise velocity. The p-th order velocity correlations follow a^((p+2)/2) for odd p and a^(p/2) for even p (a = scale factor). The fitted exponents for odd p are smaller than these predictions. The overdensity is proportional to the density correlation on the same scale, <delta> ∝ <delta delta'>; the velocity dispersion on a scale r is proportional to the overdensity on that scale. The effective viscosity of the adhesion model originates from velocity fluctuations; the negative viscosity is due to the inverse energy cascade. On small scales, a self-closed velocity evolution is obtained by splitting velocity into motion within haloes and motion of haloes. Vorticity, enstrophy and energy evolution follow from it. The mean pairwise velocity follows <Δu_L> = −H a r. The third moment follows <(Δu_L)^3> ∝ ε_u a r, with a constant energy-cascade rate ε_u ≈ −4.6×10⁻⁷ m²/s³. The combined kinematic and dynamic relations give exponential velocity correlations on large scales and one-fourth power-law correlations on small scales; the p-th order correlations follow a^((3p−5)/4) for odd p and a^(3p/4) for even p.

The reported discordance measures should not be interpreted as accident probabilities or empirical risk frequencies.

summary: Measured failure modes of verifier panels: companion paper accepted (poster) at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop Who Verifies the Agents? — Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels . Version of record: SSRN 7390698 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7390698 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://polyhelper.ai/research/agreement-not-evidence/ and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/agreement-not-evidence . Someone who asks one language model a question cannot tell a confidently wrong answer from a confidently right one. The two are identical on every surface cue available to a non-expert. Asking several models seems to solve this, but it mostly relocates the problem: reconciling several answers produces one confident text again, and that text now carries the borrowed authority of "ten of them agreed." The protocol formalized here collects answers from several consumer chat models through the user's own browser or phone, with no API keys, no installation and no intermediary server. It reconciles them by anchor-and-enrich: the strongest available answer becomes the base, and each of the others contributes only what the base lacks. Every contribution is signed with the model that supplied it. Disagreements are kept in a section of their own rather than averaged away. The paper makes four contributions. The first is the protocol itself, stated as an algorithm that preserves provenance and forbids silent deletion, together with a taxonomy of five ways a merge can fail. Four of them are defects of naive pooling; the fifth is a failure of the operator rather than of the method: a synthesis that presents a single model's output as a collegial result. The second is the application of the correlated-witness arithmetic to protocol design. That arithmetic is not claimed here. Kohli (2026) applied the same Kish correction to a panel of nine frontier judges and measured about two effective votes, and Kim et al. (2025) established the underlying error correlation across more than 350 models. A council of N models whose errors carry intraclass correlation ρ is worth = N / (1 + (N−1)ρ) independent witnesses, and that quantity saturates at 1/ρ however many models are added. Once a council is larger than 1/ρ, halving ρ beats doubling N, and a pair with low error correlation can outweigh five with high correlation. Which pairs those are is measured, not read off the label: the larger and more accurate models carry the most correlated errors even when architecture and provider differ (Kim et al., 2025), and the author's per-pair measurements found no detectable effect of geopolitical bloc on error correlation and, in the pairs measured, none of shared lineage (Chernets, 2026). The estimation procedure of Section 5.5 supplies that measurement. The third is an account of three deployment tiers, manual, one-tap mobile and browser-agent, and of the axis that separates them epistemically: whether the second model sees the first model's answer. Conditioning the second model raises ρ in exchange for error correction. The fourth is a small-sample observation of the counterfeit-council failure across five models, the one-sentence intervention that removed it in a three-model re-run, and a blinded three-arm evaluation design with a stated falsification condition. Correlated agreement is treated here as established, not as a finding. That a panel of models is worth far fewer independent witnesses than it has members has been measured directly: nine frontier judges drawn from seven families supply about two effective votes (Kohli, 2026), and error correlation rises with model capability even across providers and architectures (Kim et al., 2025). Section 5 restates the design-effect arithmetic behind those measurements, because three of the protocol's rules are derived from it and read as fastidiousness without it. The protocol then takes the other side of the same problem. That literature measures the correlation; this protocol

summary: SMaRT Transfusion  (Simplified, Meaningful and Responsible Tool for Transfusions) is a clinical decision support (CDS) tool developed at  Stanford Medicine Children's Health (SMCH)  for red blood cell (RBC) transfusion in critically ill children. It implements the consensus recommendations of the  Pediatric Critical Care Transfusion and Anemia eXpertise Initiative (TAXI) as an interactive decision tree: clinicians navigate from the patient's clinical state (hemorrhagic shock, nonhemorrhagic shock, acute respiratory failure, acute brain injury, hematologic/oncologic diagnoses, congenital or acquired heart disease, extracorporeal support, and general critical illness) through the relevant hemoglobin and physiologic thresholds to an evidence- or expert-based transfusion recommendation. It is designed for use within Epic and other EHR environments and accepts a hemoglobin value on launch to pre-seed the pathway.
title: SMaRT Transfusion: A Clinical Decision Support Tool for Red Blood Cell Transfusion in Critically Ill Children

summary: GEM Engine: Publication Dataset This dataset supports the research manuscript "GEM Engine: A reusable landscape-guided framework for exploration and optimization of genome-scale metabolic design spaces" by Hamed Rastaghi and Samuel M. D. Oliveira. GEM Engine is a computational framework designed to support reusable, landscape-guided exploration and optimization of genome-scale metabolic models. The framework combines flux balance analysis (FBA), surrogate modeling, and multi-objective optimization to enable systematic investigation of metabolic design spaces while reducing redundant simulations across optimization tasks. Dataset Contents Results.zip Contains genome-scale metabolic simulation landscapes, multi-objective optimization benchmarks, and associated computational results supporting the study. Figures_and_Tables.zip Contains data and materials associated with the main and supplementary figures and tables, including supporting analysis outputs and generation scripts where available. Reproducibility and Software The archived results support comparisons of landscape-guided optimization strategies, including gsMOBO, NSGA-II, SPARC, GHOST, and TRAIL, as well as surrogate-quality-based algorithm selection. The GEM Engine source code is maintained separately on GitHub. The repository URL will be provided when the software is publicly released.
title: GEM Engine: Simulation Landscapes and Optimization Benchmark Data for Genome-Scale Metabolic Design

summary: PICSP3D is an open-source, three-dimensional, three-velocity (3D3V) electrostatic particle-in-cell code for plasma-object interaction, such as spacecraft and probe charging, sheaths and wakes, Langmuir probes, dust grains, electrodes, magnetised plasma devices and gas discharges. Objects of arbitrary shape are embedded in a uniform Cartesian grid as signed distance functions, built from analytic primitives with constructive solid geometry or imported from CAD (STL) with generalised winding numbers. The Poisson equation is solved with a multigrid-preconditioned conjugate gradient method and second-order Shortley-Weller cut cells; floating and biased conductors are charged self-consistently through a capacitance matrix. The code includes surface processes (absorption, secondary electron emission, photoemission with self-shadowing), uniform and spatially varying static magnetic fields (dipoles, current loops, solenoids, mirrors, wires) with a Boris pusher, Monte Carlo collisions with a neutral background (elastic, charge exchange, excitation, ionisation) and binary Coulomb collisions. The solver is written in C++20 and parallelised with MPI domain decomposition and OpenMP threads; output is parallel VTK. A Python package, picsp_post, provides post-processing, figures, animations, Blender renders and a CAD import tool. The release contains the test suite, sixteen documented example cases with analysis scripts, the scaling benchmark and its results. Figures (in the repository): Logo ; CubeSat in low Earth orbit ; CubeSat ion wake ; protons trapped in a dipole field ; floating sphere and OML theory ; two-stream instability ; strong scaling on 72 cores . The full gallery and documentation are in the README .

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: identical Kuramoto oscillators scattered at random on a flat torus of any fixed dimension have stable twisted equilibria near every integer winding, which proves the twisted-equilibrium conjecture of Cirelli, Groisman, Huang and Vivas for every kernel in their class with |z|K(z) bounded. Place n identical oscillators at independent uniform points of the flat torus T d and couple points closer than ε n with weight K(z/ε n ). If ε n → 0 and nε n d+2 /log n → ∞, then with high probability, for every integer twist k with |k| ≤ c/(ε n +δ n ), where δ n = (log n/(nε n d+2 )) 1/2 , there is an asymptotically stable equilibrium whose phase differs from k·x by at most C|k|δ n at every vertex (Theorem 2.1). The kernel need only be even, supported in the unit ball, positive almost everywhere near the origin and have sup|z|K(z) finite: this covers the hard-radius graph, every bounded kernel and |z| −α , 0 < α ≤ 1. All twists k in Z d are covered, not only coordinate twists. Further results: at least c(ε n +δ n ) −d distinct stable constructed states; a basin of fixed size; for bounded radial kernels, a heat-equation limit uniform over all times; and stable weighted harmonic lifts under smooth nonuniform sampling (bounded kernels). The key tool is a sup-norm bound for the inverse graph Laplacian uniform over all conductances above a bounded backbone. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source), an exact standard-library checker of classical cycle twisted-state spectra, the numerical illustrations with their script and records, verification and claim records, preserved development drafts, two unrelated supplementary research notes kept for provenance, a rating-free internal review summary, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written informal proofs; internal AI-agent review and proof audits only (not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification); kernels with |z|K unbounded and the connectivity regime nε d ~ log n remain open; constants are not explicit; the numerics are small illustrations outside the theorem's regime. Creator: Anonymous. Text and figures CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Stable twisted equilibria on random geometric tori in every fixed dimension

summary: A staged, reproducible pipeline for VLT/MUSE narrow-field-mode integral-field data: raw-cube reduction, spectral extraction of a faint companion next to a much brighter primary star with six independent extraction schemes, and hydrogen-line accretion analysis with detection limits calibrated against empirical nulls from control positions processed identically to the object. Every stage emits a machine-readable quality-control document, and later stages read those documents rather than trusting assumptions; provenance (input cube, SHA-256 hashes, specification version, wavelength frame, flux unit) travels with the products. Research code under active development. This is the version used in Ramírez Reyes & Cáceres (in preparation).

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Two results on complementary (mutually unbiased) measurements and the complementary quantum correlation (CQC) inequality of Schneeloch, Broadbent and Howell (2014), which proposed that the classical correlations in two complementary measurement tables never exceed the quantum mutual information. 1. Sharp qutrit discrimination. For every pair of complementary bases of a qutrit and every two orthogonal states, the triangular discrimination summed over the two bases is at most 8/3 (the trivial ceiling is 4), answering Qian, arXiv:2608.14806v2, Section 11(4). Every equality case is classified; for the computational and Fourier bases they are tied to the nine Hesse SIC rays. Consequences: choosing one of the two measurements at random recovers at most two thirds of the quantum Fisher information in a two-state estimation task, and Qian's two-ray qubit-qutrit family obeys CQC with margin at least 0.1005 nats. The proof is computer-assisted: an exact rational sum-of-squares certificate (scout_qutrit/exact_sos_certificate.json, 660,609 bytes, SHA-256 825bb8108096d38a44f63f1bc91964405d189ad57b5f568530b5d8e27d598c2f) checked by a standalone exact verifier; this deposit is the certificate's citable locator. 2. Every prescribed pair fails for a qubit and a qudit of dimension n ≥ 4. For every prescribed pair of complementary measurements on each side there is a separable state violating CQC, with a uniform certified margin below −9/20,000,000 nats (previously the every-pair statement was known only for n ≥ 164). A phase-averaging extension of the known shared-label mechanism covers every prescribed pair when both dimensions are at least three; an earlier, unchecked every-pair statement for equal dimensions by E. O'Connor is credited. Open: the full qubit-qutrit CQC question and the sharp constant in dimension 5 (numerics only). The margins are tiny and structural, not experimental. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), the exact certificate and verifier, negative controls, an exact rational margin checker, numerical cross-checks, working proof notes, novelty audits, the bibliography with registry records, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: computer-assisted exact rational arithmetic, not a formal proof; internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review or independent reproduction). Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Sharp qutrit discrimination and unavoidable correlation overcounting for complementary measurements

summary: BarrierMap is a computational framework for comparing molecular permeability across the blood–brain barrier (BBB), skin, and intestinal Caco-2 systems. This record contains processed results, model summaries, cross-barrier analyses, and reproducibility materials supporting the associated manuscript. A common physicochemical descriptor baseline was combined with barrier-specific information, including ionization-derived descriptors for BBB and Caco-2 and anatomical/experimental context for skin. Predictive performance was evaluated using 20 repeated Bemis–Murcko scaffold-based train/test splits. Cross-barrier analyses were performed after molecular standardization using within-barrier percentile ranks to enable comparison among experimentally distinct permeability endpoints.
title: BarrierMap: Barrier-Specific Determinants of Molecular Permeability across Biological Interfaces

summary: This resource contains Python and Wolfram Mathematica variants of the simulation code accompanying the article Effect of Electoral Seat Bias on Political Polarization: A Computational Perspective by Daria Boratyn and Dariusz Stolicki ( International Journal of Public Opinion Research ). The code implements an agent-based Monte Carlo model designed to investigate how electoral seat bias in favor of larger parties affects the evolution of mass ideological polarization over repeated electoral cycles. The model represents voters and parties as ideal points in a two-dimensional policy space. Voter choice combines ideological proximity with preferences for larger parties, capturing strategic and bandwagon motives, and retrospective evaluations of government performance. Voter positions evolve through random preference perturbations, affective shifts associated with party attachment, and thermostatic responses to the incumbent. Electoral systems are represented by aggregate seats–votes functions: the pot-and-ladle approximation for Jefferson--D’Hondt and a power-law approximation for first-past-the-post plurality. The degree of seat bias is varied through mean district magnitude and the power-law exponent, respectively. Mass ideological polarization is measured using a modified Mehlhaff index with a degrees-of-freedom correction, with voter clusters identified through adaptive mean-shift clustering. The code is provided to facilitate inspection of the model’s assumptions and mechanisms, replication of the simulation experiments, and further computational research on the relationship between electoral institutions and political polarization.
title: Simulation Code for "Effect of Electoral Seat Bias on Political Polarization: A Computational Perspective"

summary: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection

summary: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection

summary: Standard spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks need a fixed-size adjacency matrix, coupling model weights to a specific sensor count N; they cannot produce any output at a sensor absent from training. We present OmniST, a topology-invariant forecaster whose computation has zero structural dependency on the number of nodes, and which, composed with inductive split-conformal calibration, gives distribution-free, coverage-guaranteed prediction intervals at arbitrary (including never-seen) sensor locations, preserving that guarantee as sensors are added or removed. Topology invariance follows from coordinate-based tokenization, k-nearest-neighbor attention from geographic coordinates at each forward pass, and per-node temporal processing via a bidirectional GRU. On real Delhi air-quality data (37 stations, 2019-2023), OmniST attains a 30-day PM2.5 MAE of 31.0 ug/m3 and degrades at most 1.1 percent when 40 percent of stations are removed. Its inductive forecasts at unseen stations beat nearest-neighbor interpolation (about 12 percent) and a learned kriging GNN (IGNNK, about 21 percent), and, unlike either, carry a finite-sample coverage guarantee. The guarantee holds at 90 percent or above under 30-50 percent node dropout across four real datasets over three domains (Delhi and Beijing air quality, NOAA GHCN weather, Caltrans PeMSD7-M traffic), and still holds at 325 real sensors (full PeMS-BAY). We also fix a temporal-drift failure: static conformal under-covers over time (about 0.50 late), but a rolling adaptive-conformal estimator restores target coverage (0.89 overall, 0.96 late) at the cost of wider intervals.

summary: This paper investigates whether low-order packet-loss statistics suffice to assess survival-time risk under bursty packet losses, i.e., the probability that no update succeeds for a prescribed number of consecutive slots. Conventional models, such as the Gilbert model, characterize packet losses using the loss rate and mean burst length, but channels sharing these statistics may exhibit substantially different failure risks. We characterize the Markov channels one order above a given low-order fit that share its statistics and analyze their risks under acknowledgment-based scheduling with transmission budgets. We show that, with dense transmission attempts, risk is primarily governed by loss persistence beyond the modeled memory, and the worst-case channel need not be the most persistent one. Under limited budgets, retry spacing makes loss relapse probabilities important and can reverse the risk ordering of compatible channels. Numerical and measurement results show that low-order models can substantially underestimate the risk, highlighting the need for scheduling-dependent channel statistics.
title: Survival-Time Risk Beyond Low-Order Channel Models: Identifiability and Scheduling

summary: Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model. Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.
title: Dr. No: Feature Steering for Abstention in Vision-Language Models

summary: This record contains the rights-safe reproducibility package supporting the manuscript “Observed agreement is not decision portability: A typed evidence-authority audit of national renewable-energy priorities.” The study distinguishes retrospective cross-country recurrence from source-to-target decision authority. Stage I freezes a retrospective calibration corpus of 14 reports and 15 study units. Stage II contains three sequential outcome-blinded validation blocks with 25 exact technology relations. Context-blind transfer issued 11 certificates: four correct and seven incorrect (coverage 0.440; conditional agreement 0.364; false-portability rate 0.636). The criterion-resolved bounded rule issued no positive certificate across 13 applicable opportunities; this is reported as zero coverage and disciplined abstention, not predictive superiority. The Scopus component contains a frozen 1,363-record title/abstract universe. Of 251 full-text candidates, 110 received full-text-stage decisions across 13 dated batches; 49 were map eligible, 61 were excluded and 141 remained unassessed because exhaustive full-text census completion was not an objective. Acquisition ordering and stopping were documented but not preregistered. Later map-eligible records were not retroactively added to the already frozen Stage I calibration corpus. Copyrighted article PDFs, extracted article text, licensed Scopus exports, browser sessions, credentials and institutional-access artifacts are excluded. summary: Social support is an essential protective factor against the risk of talent development failure, especially in the catastrophic situation. This study aimed to test the validity and reliability of social support instruments specifically for talented sports students in Malaysia. Content validity index (CVI), exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and internal consistency are the methods used to ensure that measurement instruments are appropriate for use in local contexts and cultures. A total of 268 from four talented sports students aged 16 years were selected by proportionate stratified random sampling in this study. The study found that the instrument had good content validity, with the items reaching the minimum level of CVI value and exceeding the recommended cut-off point of 0.78. Factor analysis found that the final measurement model has three factors, namely i) family support, ii) friends' support, and iii) coach support, with factor loading ranging between 0.49 and 0.89. The correlation matrix was also measured through the KMO and Bartlett test of sphericity. All three factors had internal consistency values of 0.83 for coach support and 0.85 for family and friend support, which was defined as good. Future research is warranted to explore the instrument with different samples and measurements in various scenarios.

summary: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.
title: WASP-Mem: Let Agent Organize Procedural Memory. Human Spend Effort on Diagnosis

summary: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) processes temporal information through quantum dynamics, but it remains unclear whether small QRC models can forecast real data competitively with classical models and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. We address both questions for a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. Five reservoir candidates were selected and frozen using hardware-native interaction graphs, Trotterized Ising dynamics, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. On 232 held-out test days, the ideal candidates reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66-6.12 claims/day, compared with 5.36 for ridge regression. For four of the five, the difference from ridge was not significant under a 95% block bootstrap, and their accuracy was comparable with classical recurrent and reservoir baselines. On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor, we ran 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds, comparing hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization level 1 layouts. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with a maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), and avoided the severe transfer failures seen for some random layouts. Most of the hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short hardware probe on training inputs detected before the test runs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without a consistent gain in forecasting accuracy or hardware transfer. Small QRC models can thus reach competitive accuracy on this task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent.
title: Hardware-Aware Design and Layout Selection in Quantum Reservoir Computing for Insurance Claims Forecasting

summary: Retrieval-augmented Web applications increasingly employ multi-agent debate (MAD) to aggregate conflicting, noisy, and heterogeneous information, yet deliberation is fundamentally a social process susceptible to interpersonal dynamics. When retrieved Web sources contain latent hazards alongside safe factual content, social biases such as conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries. In this work, we investigate whether the social structure of deliberation can paradoxically amplify latent Web safety risks. We introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six core Web risk categories, which holds queries and retrieved evidence strictly invariant while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Empirical evaluation across diverse proprietary and open-source backbones reveals that while isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, standard MAD catastrophically capitulates to social pressure---surging unsafe adoption from 0.0\% up to 100.0\% and systematically silencing safe minority evidence. To resolve this systemic fragility without retraining or debate regeneration, we propose RiskTrace-Debias, an inference-time auditing framework uniting evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to $\le 2.0\%$ across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, while generating verifiable provenance traces to audit interpersonal manipulation in Web deliberation.
title: When Debate Amplifies Risk: Social-Bias Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent Safety Deliberation

summary: Can an LLM directly edit the weights of a diffusion-based image-restoration model to \emph{improve} restoration quality---without gradients, paired data, or fine-tuning? Recent experiments show frontier LLMs can fix structural bugs by modifying as little as \(0.016\%\) of parameters, but cannot instill new capabilities. We ask whether weight-space programming (WSP) can move from \emph{debugging} to \emph{improvement} in the precise-regression setting of image restoration (deblurring, super-resolution, denoising, inpainting). Restoration diffusion UNets present a middle ground: low-level signal-processing layers are concentrated enough for targeted weight-direction edits, while high-level semantic layers remain distributed and resistant to sparse modification. We propose three technical conjectures: (C1) an LLM can localize the layer behind a quality gap (over-smoothing, color shift, hallucinated texture) within a 200 forward-pass budget; (C2) editing a small set of identified weight directions (e.g., scaling high-frequency filter norms, correcting output-bias channels) can measurably improve PSNR and perceptual quality; (C3) a recursive loop---diagnose \(\rightarrow\) edit \(\rightarrow\) evaluate \(\rightarrow\) re-diagnose---can compound gains across rounds, forming a minimal recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop for vision. We analyze the required AI capability (arguing targeted edits need not superintelligence, while general capability generation does) and detail the challenges of precise pixel-level regression. We provide a PyTorch-style deployment pipeline and outline a benchmark. This manuscript is conjectural, intended to open a new subtopic for image restoration.
title: Weight-Space Programming for Improving Image-Restoration Diffusion Models: Technical Conjectures and a Recursive Improvement Loop

summary: Graph databases are often used to manage relationship-rich data, whose graph structure and attributes may be sensitive. In many applications, a database owner or a service provider evaluates queries over a private graph for a client. Because the graph cannot be fully disclosed and independently re-executing the query may be impractical, the client cannot directly verify the returned result. This creates a need for verifiable graph query evaluation that preserves data confidentiality. We present VerfGraph, a zero-knowledge system for verifiable graph query evaluation, which enables a client to verify that the query result was correctly computed over a committed graph data, without revealing private graph records or intermediate query values beyond the public inputs and what is implied by the query result. Building on the expansion-centric model introduced by the state-of-the-art zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation system ZKGraph (ICDE'26), VerfGraph achieves more efficient and expressive zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation by advancing design in two key ways. First, we propose novel operator-proof methods for core expansion and shortest-path operations that reduce costly sorting and comparison checks and eliminate edge canonicalization for bidirectional expansion. Furthermore, we introduce correctness proofs for count and weighted shortest-path operators, broadening the class of graph queries that can be verified. We evaluate VerfGraph using the LDBC Social Network Benchmark. Compared with ZKGraph on complex IC queries, VerfGraph achieves $33.9\times$-$59.7\times$ speedups in proof generation and reduces peak prover memory by factors of $4.5\times$-$6.6\times$, while maintaining millisecond-level verification and producing sub-MB proofs.
title: VerfGraph: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Verifiable Graph Query Evaluation System

Building on the expansion-centric model introduced by the state-of-the-art zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation system ZKGraph (ICDE'26), VerfGraph achieves more efficient and expressive zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation by advancing design in two key ways. First, we propose novel operator-proof methods for core expansion and shortest-path operations that reduce costly sorting and comparison checks and eliminate edge canonicalization for bidirectional expansion. Furthermore, we introduce correctness proofs for count and weighted shortest-path operators, broadening the class of graph queries that can be verified. We evaluate VerfGraph using the LDBC Social Network Benchmark. Compared with ZKGraph on complex IC queries, VerfGraph achieves $33.9\times$-$59.7\times$ speedups in proof generation and reduces peak prover memory by factors of $4.5\times$-$6.6\times$, while maintaining millisecond-level verification and producing sub-MB proofs.
title: VerfGraph: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Verifiable Graph Query Evaluation System

summary: Frontier LLM agents can turn known vulnerabilities into working exploits, but are costly and often access-restricted due to their potential for malicious use. Open-weight models offer a more accessible alternative, but struggle to maintain progress across long exploitation chains. They also often fail to apply relevant security knowledge at the appropriate stage and in the right context to identify and evaluate promising attack directions. To address these limitations, we propose DoGNAVY-Exploit, a multi-agent harness built around two complementary designs: stage-aware decomposition with progressive expert knowledge disclosure, and hierarchical orchestration with parallel exploration. Specifically, DoGNAVY-Exploit uses configurable milestones to recast long-horizon exploitation as short, verifiable capability transitions and provides only the knowledge relevant to each stage. Within each milestone, a hierarchical architecture separates strategic planning from parallel execution: a planner proposes diverse attack routes, executors test them concurrently, and a controller accepts progress only when supported by runtime evidence. A shared structured memory consolidates verified facts, artifacts, replay steps, and failed routes across branches, allowing agents to build on collective progress and carry validated knowledge into subsequent milestones. In controlled benchmark environments, DoGNAVY-Exploit with GLM-5.2 achieves 97.5% Pass@1 on Cybench, and 97.5% zero-day and 100% one-day Pass@1 on CVE-Bench. On ExploitGym, it solves 79 tasks with GLM-5.2 and 157 with GLM-5.3, while the corresponding public Claude Code baselines solve 39 and 130 tasks, respectively. Ablation results further demonstrate that the stage-aware orchestration, expert knowledge, parallel exploration, and memory designs can substantially improve the exploitation capabilities of open-weight agents.
title: DoGNAVY-Exploit: Harnessing Parallel Open-Weight Agents for Stage-Aware Vulnerability Exploitation

summary: This dataset contains raw and processed data supporting the development and validation of phasor-based spectral flow cytometry (phSFC). This framework extends spectral phasor analysis, traditionally used in hyperspectral microscopy, to high-throughput flow cytometry, enabling model-free visualization and quantification of complex fluorescent signals. Archives all_data.zip: the complete dataset (all raw, pre-gated and technical benchmark files, for spectral flow cytometry and hyperspectral microscopy), organized as described below. source_data_fig_1.zip: Source Data for Figure 1. source_data_fig_2.zip: Source Data for Figure 2. source_data_extended_data_fig_1.zip: Source Data for Extended Data Figure 1. The three Source Data archives contain copies of the files from all_data.zip that are needed to reproduce the corresponding figure. Each one is organized in folders named after the figure panel they feed, so each figure can be reproduced without downloading the full dataset. Files used by more than one figure (for example, the MLV and BAL pre-gated files) are included in each archive that uses them. Dataset Contents The record is organized by experimental model, technical validation benchmarks, and acquisition modality: Multilamellar Vesicles (MLVs): Data of DOPC, DPPC, and Cholesterol mixtures labeled with LAURDAN. Used for cross-modal validation and establishing reference phasor coordinates for membrane order. Vero Cell Culture: Data from live cells treated with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) to induce cholesterol depletion. Includes an OLS Unmixed subfolder containing raw data unmixed via the ordinary least-squares algorithm. Ex Vivo Leukocytes: Data from a mouse model of lung inflammation (LPS-induced). Contains multi-color spectral flow cytometry data (LAURDAN + CD11c + CD45) from bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL). Flow Rate Analysis: Whole blood cells stained with Hoechst and CD45-BV510, acquired across variable throughput regimes (Low, Medium, and Fast sample flow rates) to benchmark phasor coordinate stability. Gain Analysis: Unstained Vero cells acquired under systematic detector gain attenuation (-20%, -40%, -60%, and -80%) to evaluate robustness against signal dynamic range shifts. Data Organization & File Formats To ensure reproducibility and transparency, the files in all_data.zip are categorized as follows: Spectral Flow Cytometry (.fcs): Ungated Folder: Raw acquisition files directly exported from the Cytek Aurora. Pre-gated Folder: Files containing specific populations (e.g., singlets, LAURDAN+ events, or specific cell subsets) exported following the gating workflows described in the Methods. Technical Benchmarks: Dedicated folders for Flow rate analysis, Gain analysis, and OLS Unmixed files. Hyperspectral Microscopy (.lsm): Raw Data: Original hyperspectral stacks. Masks Folder: Binary masks (stored as image files) used to restrict analysis to specific regions of interest (ROIs), such as vesicle membranes or cellular boundaries. The Source Data archives contain only spectral flow cytometry files (.fcs), taken from the Pre-gated folders, the Flow rate analysis and Gain analysis folders, and, for Figure 2d, one file from the Ungated folder. Technical Specifications Spectral Flow Cytometry: Acquired on a Cytek Aurora (3-laser configuration). Spectral range analyzed: 428–812 nm (16 channels, Violet excitation). Hyperspectral Microscopy: Acquired on a Zeiss LSM 880 in Lambda Mode (63×/1.4 NA). Spectral range: 423–693 nm (28 channels, 10 nm spacing). Processing & Analysis: Initial gating and traditional unmixing performed in FlowJo / SpectroFlo. Downstream spectral phasor transformations, component calculations, and visualization performed using the PhasorPy library in Python.
title: Dataset for phSFC framework: Spectral Flow Cytometry and Hyperspectral Confocal Microscopy Files

summary: Wearable sports sensors can recognize actions on the device itself, where lower-precision numbers reduce model storage and memory traffic. Two 4-bit block-scaled formats, MXFP4 from the Open Compute Project, introduced in 2023, and NVFP4 from NVIDIA, introduced in 2025, are drawing interest. Published evaluations cover general deep-learning benchmarks and large language models; to our knowledge, nobody has yet measured what they cost a small wearable-sensor model. We train a 159,492-parameter 1D CNN to recognize four basketball actions from wrist-accelerometer data in Hang-Time HAR and test it on players it has never seen, using five-fold cross-validation grouped by player. Every comparison between number formats is made fold by fold. In full precision the model reaches 69.26\% macro-F1. Measured TFLite FP16 and INT8 models lose at most 0.16 percentage points. In simulation, 4-bit weights cost 1.45 points with MXFP4 and 0.72 points with NVFP4. When activations are quantized to 4 bits as well, MXFP4 loses 5.14 points and NVFP4 only 0.75, and NVFP4 comes out ahead in all five held-out-player folds. The ranking survives two alternative simulator settings, with NVFP4 leading by 3.49 to 4.40 points. A $2 \times 3$ ablation with 4-bit weights and activations (two block sizes and three scale rules) points to scale selection as the main source of MXFP4's loss. The reference MXFP4 conversion we simulate rounds the scale down, which can pick scales that are too small, so many blocks clip their largest values. Rounding the scale up recovers 3.18 points with 32-value blocks and 3.63 points with 16-value blocks, and switching to an 8-bit floating-point scale, as NVFP4 does, adds another 0.84 and 1.20 points. Block size matters less. Under this round-down rule, 16-value blocks score 0.44 points below 32-value blocks in all five folds; under the other two rules there is no consistent effect.
title: What Does 4-Bit Microscaling Cost a Wearable Activity Recognizer?

summary: Mainstream sequence-processing AI is temporally reactive: each update is driven by input and learned state transitions, rather than by an independently evolving internal temporal reference. Biological brains, by contrast, continuously generate rhythmic activity that structures perception, memory, and cognition, and this rhythmicity reaches all the way to behavior. We ask whether this difference is merely implementational or genuinely computational. Four lines of evidence suggest that endogenous temporal structure supports putative functions that input-driven architectures may not readily replicate: 1) phase-dependent routing of information, 2) delay-structured combinatorial representation, 3) cross-frequency multiplexing of items, and 4) oscillation-gated offline consolidation. A proof-of-concept delay-ablation test dissociates representational capacity from memory retrieval. In recurrent and spatial spiking networks with fixed synaptic weights and connectivity, shuffling delays preserves part of the capacity but substantially impairs the sequence retrieval. The relative contrast is more pronounced for spatial networks and longer propagations. Instantaneous transmission collapses capacity itself. We then outline a cross-frequency multiplexing scheme that combines item identity and serial order with alternative mechanisms for selective memory retrieval. Finally, we state one falsifiable hypothesis, conditions for matched-resource tests, and three research directions: the components already exist; the disciplined comparison does not.
title: Clocks all the way down: does sequence-processing AI need endogenous temporal structure?

summary: Long-horizon video generation is increasingly moving toward autoregressive rollout, where each newly generated segment becomes part of the evidence used for future prediction. Recent causal decoders, long-context training, and KV-cache mechanisms have extended feasible duration, but most inference pipelines still decide the visible past implicitly through recent windows, compressed caches, or external memory. This raises a direct question: \textbf{can the choice of which past frames or segments to show to the decoder be treated as an explicit test-time decision?} We answer this question with \textsc{ReCR}, a training-free method that formulates autoregressive video decoding as representation-guided context rewriting. At each step, \textsc{ReCR} builds a selected visible context from the generated history by using internal decoder representations to favor context units that match the global rollout state, avoid redundancy with the recent continuation, preserve temporal boundary coverage, and widen the range of spatial layouts in view. The selected units are then mapped onto a compact causal axis before decoding the next block. Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, \textsc{ReCR} consistently improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets. Empirical analyses such as representation-space diagnostics and transition-count prompt switching further show that improving what remains visible is an effective path toward more stable long-video decoding.
title: What Remains in Sight? Autoregressive Video Decoding as Representation-Guided Context Rewriting

summary: Looped transformers apply a shared block several times per token to improve accuracy without adding parameters. For models such as Ouro that keep a separate key-value (KV) cache per loop, cache memory limits the batch size that amortizes repeated weight reads. Uniform-bit quantization and fixed rules per loop do not allocate precision according to each layer's sensitivity in each loop. Measurements on Ouro show that quantization sensitivity varies across (loop, layer) cells, and the sum of individual cell damages approximates the overall output damage. Sharing damage also varies by cell, with later loops generally tolerating sharing better. Skipping low-attention values to save reads produces errors that compound across loops. LoopKV uses a one-time offline profile to choose 4-bit storage, 2-bit storage or reuse of the final loop's KV for each cell. The planner minimizes reads under budgets for predicted damage and storage. During decoding, each loop reads the high 2 bits of each 4-bit value and fetches the low bits only where its own attention weights require 4-bit precision. A single fused kernel in vLLM executes the plan. Serving Ouro-1.4B on one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized LoopKV-M plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit quantization (KIVI-4) on the same fused kernel and CUDA graph. It sustains 1.7-2.2x KIVI-4's goodput under a latency service-level objective with a 16K-token maximum length. None of its averages on six public benchmarks falls significantly below BF16's.
title: LoopKV: Loop-Aware KV Cache Compression for Serving Looped Transformers

summary: Under temporal nonstationarity, model performance rankings reverse across training horizons due to heterogeneous sensitivities to memory. While existing literature addresses adaptive lookbacks, effective model complexity, and empirical forecast evaluation in isolation, no unified framework explains the structural mechanics driving these rank reversals. We bridge this gap by deriving a model-agnostic decomposition of out-of-sample $R^2$ into target alignment, miscalibrated aggressiveness, and predictive instability. Within this framework, we mathematically characterize complexity phase boundaries, establish closed-form optimal-memory equations for ridge regression under local drift, and extend these guarantees to complex model architectures via surrogate bounds. We validate these theoretical dynamics by benchmarking 14 linear, tree-based, and neural architectures across large-scale financial panels. In doing so, our framework demonstrates that empirical model rank reversals are driven by predictable surges in miscalibrated aggressiveness, providing a rigorous mechanistic diagnosis of generalization under temporal shift.
title: Decomposing Rank Reversals under Temporal Nonstationarity: Alignment, Aggressiveness, and Instability

summary: To enable effective generalization in offline meta-RL, it is essential to accurately infer the underlying task through latent task representations, which provide a compact and transferable summary of task-specific characteristics for guiding policy generation. In this paper, we propose Contrastive Task-Aware Decision Transformer (CoTA-DT), a DT-based offline meta-RL framework that learns task representations by jointly integrating four complementary components: (i) contrastive learning from offline trajectories, (ii) alignment with natural-language task descriptions, (iii) one-step supervision via a task-conditioned world model, and (iv) long-term supervision via a task-conditioned Q function. The learned task representations are used as conditioning signals for a DT-based policy, enabling task-aware meta-policy learning. To further support generalization in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, we design a language-grounded, self-adaptive strategy that enables effective and reliable adaptation to unseen tasks. Notably, in CoTA-DT, the pretrained LLM serves as a shared backbone for language encoding, world modeling, Q-function estimation, and policy learning. This unified design facilitates parameter sharing, improving both efficiency and generalization. Extensive experiments across diverse offline meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate that CoTA-DT consistently outperforms prior methods, particularly in challenging zero-shot generalization scenarios.
title: Decision Transformer with Task-Aware Representations for Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning

summary: Modern learning systems increasingly combine pretrained models with downstream heads. Despite the growing importance of such modular designs, how the downstream model co-adapts to the geometry of pretrained representations remains relatively underexplored. We study this problem through vision-language-action models (VLAs), where a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) conditions an action model for control. We find that the action model progressively concentrates its sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of the VLM outputs. Through controlled experiments across different backbone-head models, we further show that counteracting this sensitivity concentration can be beneficial under representation--task mismatch settings. Motivated by these observations, we introduce \emph{Adaptive Interface Equalizer} (AdaIE), a parameter-free mechanism that reweights pretrained representations according to the evolving downstream sensitivity during training. AdaIE improves VLA success rates on simulation benchmarks, with gains of up to $+5.28$ percentage points (pp) on RoboCasa-GR1 and $+1.68$ pp on RoboTwin 2.0, and achieves an average gain of $+19$ pp across five real-world manipulation tasks. It further generalizes to diffusion policies and world models, improving downstream performance in both settings. Our results highlight interface co-adaptation as an important optimization problem when coupling pretrained representations with downstream models.
title: Controlling Action-Head Co-Adaptation to VLM Representation Anisotropy

summary: Fast Dominance Estimation Clustering (FastDEC) is an efficient variant of Density Peak Clustering (DPC) that achieves high clustering quality through dominance-based density estimation, but remains constrained by the computational cost of exact k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) construction and dominance component (DC) processing. We present SymWarp-FastDEC, a GPU-accelerated implementation of FastDEC. At its core is SymTrikNN, an exact self-k-NN kernel that exploits search symmetry using upper-triangular traversal and warp-cooperative top-k selection. We also introduce WP-DC, a warp-parallel DC reduction algorithm designed for modern GPUs. Combined with memory-adaptive execution planning and stream scheduling, WP-DC eliminates DC reduction as a runtime bottleneck. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that SymWarp-FastDEC produces clustering outputs identical to the original FastDEC on all evaluated equivalence benchmarks. Compared with a FastDEC variant using FAISS GpuIndexFlatL2 for exact k-NN search, our approach achieves approximately 1.7x to 4.9x higher end-to-end performance, with the advantage generally increasing with dimensionality. Compared with the original single-threaded Python FastDEC implementation, speedups reach approximately 2.5 x 10^4 in a very high-dimensional case where its k-d-tree-based search degrades; this extreme result is not representative of typical acceleration.
title: Accelerating FastDEC Clustering Algorithm with GPUs

summary: A stored experience may answer one future question and offer little help with another. We measure this task-conditioned utility rather than assigning each memory a single importance score. A task-blind writer stores a memory without seeing the later task; a frozen reader then answers that task with and without the memory, using identical filler. A cost ledger records the resources used to form, store and expose the memory. On single-call factual-recall tasks built from LongMemEval-V2 web-agent memories, the same memory helps more when it contains information needed for the answer. Its mean paired reward gain on these answer-bearing task pairs exceeds that on matched-control pairs by $+0.33$ (95% interval $+0.21$ to $+0.46$). The tested task-blind summaries and structured records yield smaller gains than Raw, including at fixed total context; a budget sweep is consistent with retention of answer-bearing content contributing to the difference. The bearing--control contrast remains positive in a new session with randomized memory position and under a second reader, although individual memory--task labels change. Generic retrieval performs above chance but misses most screen-defined answer-bearing memories. The factual-recall gains do not extend to the tested software-engineering and scientific-coding benchmarks, where even raw memories have no measurable effect. We provide a public, versioned Conditional Memory Utility Dataset of paired measurements and costs. The practical takeaway is to evaluate memory compression by the task utility it preserves alongside its costs. Task-conditioned measurements make this comparison possible; their stability must also be checked.
title: What Is This Memory Useful For? Measuring Task-Conditioned Utility in Long-Term Agent Memory

summary: Speech watermarking is becoming a key defense for digital copyright and content authentication. Existing attacks treat evasion as a removal problem: they erase the watermark, relying on detector access or on speech data that is hard to collect, such as paired clean-watermarked or clean target speaker speech. Commercial platforms are moving to close off these assumptions. TrustedAudio, for instance, restricts detection to authenticated users and denies meaningful detection feedback to unauthorized parties. Adversaries thus cannot tell whether a sample is watermarked or which watermark it carries, nor reliably remove it without degrading speech quality. In this work, we show that evading a speech watermark does not require erasing it: detection relies on the structural consistency of the embedded pattern, and disrupting this consistency is enough to defeat it. Building on this observation, we identify harmonic structure as an effective attack surface, as perturbing it breaks watermark consistency while preserving perceptual quality. We therefore propose ScrambleMark, a zero-query, watermark-agnostic, black-box attack that evades detection through harmonic scrambling. ScrambleMark combines a deterministic engine for discovering transferable harmonic perturbations with a generative model that learns randomized scrambling patterns, avoiding reliance on fixed attack rules. Across three commercial platforms (Google SynthID, Resemble AI, and TrustedAudio), ScrambleMark is the only attack to both evade detection and keep speech natural, achieving nearly 97% evasion and a 4.2/5 human rating, far above the 1.1 to 1.7 of prior attacks. Beyond evasion, ScrambleMark withstands adaptive recovery designed to reverse it, evidence that structural evasion is hard to mitigate in practice.
title: ScrambleMark: Zero-Query Watermark-Agnostic Black-Box Evasion of Modern Speech Watermarking

summary: Prestress governs the stability, stiffness, and dynamic behavior of tensegrity structures, but it is not directly observable from sparse structural measurements, and it may decrease during service life. Under strong excitation, the cables may slacken and the dynamics become nonsmooth. Existing identification methods are limited to the taut regime, and physics-informed networks for tensegrities solve only the forward problem of predicting the response from known member parameters. This study formulates the inverse problem. Neural networks are trained on the equation-of-motion residual in constrained Cartesian coordinates, where the mass matrix is constant and the force densities enter linearly. The force densities, damping, and axial stiffness are trainable parameters, and the tension-only cable law is kept. A Fisher-information analysis shows, before inversion, which member parameters a record can determine. The method is tested on simulated planar tensegrity frames with up to five modules and a three-dimensional prism, and on measured records of a biomimetic leg and a full-scale tensegrity simplex. On the one-module frame, the identifiable force densities are recovered within 1.5% from noisy accelerations at half the free coordinates, on records with and without taut-slack transitions. Records with transitions determine members that taut records leave undetermined. On the five-module frame, a 16-cable two-span bridge, the median force-density error rises moderately, to 4.2%. On measured records, an identified spring stiffness is within 0.1% of its independently measured value on average, and the identified simplex prestress at 13 levels agrees with its cable force transducers to 2.9% root-mean-square.
title: Physics-Informed Identification of Tensegrity Prestress across Taut-Slack Transitions

summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is expected to observe gravitational-wave signals from massive black hole binaries, extreme mass ratio inspirals, and more. Despite the significant scientific potential, accurately extracting these signals from the data will only be possible if LISA's instrumental noise is understood: poor noise modelling will result in lost signals, biased parameter estimates, and incorrect astrophysical insights. Modelling LISA's instrumental noise is more challenging than its ground-based counterpart since the data is highly correlated, meaning that the noise covariance matrix can no longer be assumed diagonal in frequency and in the different data streams. In this work, we present an initial approach to perform non-parametric noise inference for LISA that requires no prior knowledge of the LISA observatory. By fitting the full noise covariance matrix with a combination of splines and inverse Lorentzians, we show that our model can estimate the power and cross spectral densities for LISA from 7 days of simulated noise-only data. We find that the median estimate from our non-parametric model whitens the data according to the expected unit normal distribution. We envision that our non-parametric model can be used as part of the global fit, as well as in combination with modelled approaches to identify, quantify, and constrain the frequency dependence of unknown noise artifacts.
title: Noisy pipelines II: Non-parametric Noise Inference for LISA

summary: Woody Crown Hydraulic Network (WCHN): mathematical revisions, corrected datasets, and reproducible computational resources This repository provides an integrated historical, mathematical, empirical, and computational resource for the Woody Crown Hydraulic Network (WCHN) framework. It brings together the foundational development of the model, revised property definitions and their algebraic consequences, corrected crown-network records, ecological reanalyses, editable network drawings, and software for reconstructing and analyzing existing or newly constructed WCHNs. The deposit is an independent scientific resource, not tied to a particular journal or manuscript. HISTORICAL FOUNDATION Four publications document the model's development: (1) Souza et al. (2011), the original network analysis of Cerrado crowns ( https://doi.org/10.1007/s11258-010-9797-7 ); (2) Prado et al. (2020), formalization of decomposition, topology, and four initial properties ( https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2020.110318 ); (3) Prado and Trovão (2023), expansion to eight properties and Caatinga–Cerrado comparisons ( https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2023.110345 ); and (4) Prado (2024), stochastic node-addition networks and size-matched comparisons ( https://doi.org/10.1007/s40626-024-00340-5 ). These references allow users to trace the original definitions and later revisions. MATHEMATICAL AND EMPIRICAL CONTENT The author-prepared document “Algebraic relationships and mathematical properties of the Woody Crown Hydraulic Network” explains the revised symmetry (SYM), complexity (COM), and vulnerability (VUL) definitions, algebraic dependencies, network-size effects, and reproducibility checks. In particular, revised VUL is exactly equal to normalized mean node depth in a rooted tree. The observed near-reciprocity between navigability (NAV) and VUL is a strong empirical association, not a second exact identity or independent hydraulic measurement. The deposit retains the original Cerrado and Caatinga source spreadsheets, recalculated property tables, comparisons, reduced principal component analyses (PCAs), and size-adjusted exploratory analyses. The previously deposited PCA outputs are preserved numerically; their interpretations should account for the revised mathematical meaning of VUL. The updated PCA technical note documents the analytical methods and limitations. CORRECTED CERRADO NETWORKS AND TOOLKIT A new workbook records corrections to 20 previously sampled Cerrado WCHNs (not additional independent observations). Six networks were reconstructed manually, including S. polyphyllum 1 as the manual feasibility pilot; fourteen were reconstructed semi-automatically, beginning with S. camporum 1 as the first test of the connector generator, followed by thirteen additional networks. In the semi-automatic workflow, the researcher marked the nodes, deterministic software proposed editable connectors and highlighted ambiguous nodes in red, and the researcher visually checked and corrected the complete graph against the original drawing beneath it. The WCHN toolkit v1.0.3 contains code, documentation, editable PowerPoint networks, intermediate files, tests, and a separate semi-automatic validation exercise using Miconia albicans 5, a network originally reconstructed manually. That exercise led to a verified terminal-connector decomposition correction without changing the network topology or any of its eight WCHN properties. The accompanying Practical Guide v1.0.3 provides step-by-step instructions for reconstructing, inspecting, validating, and analyzing WCHNs, including optional AI assistance under mandatory researcher supervision. REPRODUCIBILITY AND LIMITATIONS The accompanying README.md provides the complete file inventory, foundational references, directions for reusing the toolkit and statistical scripts, links among materials, and version history. These resources enable checking corrected topologies and calculations and exploring
title: Recalculated woody crown hydraulic network properties and reduced principal component analyses of Caatinga and Cerrado trees
